chapter_title: Inheritance and Polymorphism in Unreal Engine

screens.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism in Unreal Engine
screens.subtitle: Reuse, extend, and vary behavior across game objects using C++ class hierarchies

narration.text: In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of inheritance and polymorphism as they work inside Unreal Engine. You will see why creating base classes like AEnemy or AWeapon lets you share common data and logic across many specialized actors, and why polymorphism — calling a function through a base-class pointer that actually runs a derived-class implementation — is essential for flexible game systems. We will walk through concrete C++ examples that use virtual functions and pure virtual functions to define overridable behavior, and we'll show how the override keyword protects you from subtle mistakes. You will also learn practical pitfalls to avoid, such as function hiding, object slicing, and attempting to instantiate abstract classes. Finally, you will be guided through a hands-on weapon example where a weapon manager calls Fire() on a collection of AWeapon pointers and sees rifle and pistol behavior occur without conditional logic. By the end of this chapter you will understand both the theory and a straightforward pattern you can reuse when designing enemies, pickups, weapons, and gameplay systems in Unreal. Think about one actor type you want to generalize — this lesson will give you the vocabulary and code patterns to do that safely.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Define behavior in base classes and vary it in derived classes using virtual functions; use polymorphism so game systems operate on common interfaces rather than concrete types.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Inheritance & Polymorphism

Learn why Unreal's class hierarchy and virtual functions let you write extensible gameplay systems with minimal conditionals.

In this lesson

Understand inheritance, use polymorphism with virtual functions, implement pure virtual interfaces, and follow the override best practice in Unreal Engine C++.

Why it matters

These patterns remove duplicated code and let the engine call actor-specific logic such as BeginPlay and Tick through base pointers, enabling scalable, maintainable game code.

Getting started

Pick a gameplay concept to generalize: enemy, weapon, or collectible. We'll show code patterns and a short hands-on example you can reproduce in your project.

Hierarchy Snapshot
UObject → AActor → ACharacter → AM yPlayerCharacter
Base class defines shared state and behavior like Health and MovementSpeed.
Derived classes specialize behavior, overriding virtual functions where needed.
Explore Key Topics
Inheritance: structure types into logical hierarchies and reuse code across specialized actors.
Polymorphism: call the correct derived behavior through base pointers at runtime.
Best practices: use override and pure virtual functions to define interfaces and catch errors early.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do — part 1
screens.subtitle: Core skills and measurable outcomes for this chapter

narration.text: These objectives specify the concrete abilities you'll leave this chapter with. First, you'll understand inheritance: what it means for one class to be derived from another and why that creates an "is-a" relationship useful for organizing gameplay code. Second, you'll apply polymorphism: you'll be able to write code that treats different actor types the same through a base pointer or reference and let the runtime pick the correct behavior. Third, you'll learn to recognize and differentiate virtual functions — methods in a base class that permit runtime overriding. Fourth, you'll learn about pure virtual functions and how they make a class abstract, forcing derived classes to implement required behavior. Each objective includes a small reason why it matters and a simple mnemonic to help you remember the pattern. Consider which of your current project systems could become a base class; that will make these objectives immediately practical.

keyIdea.title: Objectives snapshot
keyIdea.text: Master the vocabulary and patterns: inheritance, polymorphism, virtual, and pure virtual — with immediate code examples you can reuse.

screens.title: What you'll be able to do — part 2
screens.subtitle: Practical skills and engineering cautions to adopt

narration.text: Continuing the objectives, you'll implement and override virtual functions in Unreal C++ classes using the override keyword to let the compiler catch signature mistakes. You will learn to recognize common pitfalls: forgetting to declare a function virtual, which prevents polymorphic behavior, and object slicing that destroys derived-specific data when passing by value. You will also complete a hands-on activity: create a base AWeapon actor with a virtual Fire method, then make ARifle and APistol derived classes that override Fire, and verify polymorphism by calling Fire through AWeapon pointers. These objectives are practical: they move from concept to a simple reproducible pattern you can use in your project. As you study, identify one class in your game that could be a base, and plan a small derived type that changes only the overridden behavior.

keyIdea.title: Practice-oriented goals
keyIdea.text: Use override to protect your intent, avoid slicing by using pointers, and build small base classes that define contracts for derived types.

screens.title: Inheritance: code reuse and "is-a" relationships
screens.subtitle: How derived classes inherit data and behavior from a base class

narration.text: Inheritance creates a relationship where one class is defined in terms of another, giving derived classes the fields and functions of their base class and allowing specialization. In Unreal you see this everywhere: UObject is the root, and AActor extends that root to add world presence and lifecycle events. When you design a base AEnemy class you can put properties like Health, MovementSpeed, and common functions like TakeDamage and Attack there, and every concrete enemy type reuses that logic without repeating code. For example, AZombieEnemy inherits AEnemy and therefore gains the Health field and any utility functions, then adds zombie-specific logic like a bite or slow effect. This structure reduces redundancy, centralizes shared behavior, and makes changes easier: adjust the base class once and all derived types benefit. A common misconception is that inheritance equals code duplication prevention only; in practice it also encodes game domain relationships and enables polymorphism—the ability to treat many derived types through a single base type. When modeling in-game entities, prefer narrow, focused base classes that define a clear contract. Resist making a single monolithic base that accumulates unrelated features. A concise base with well-defined responsibilities gives you clean reuse and safer overrides in derived actors.

keyIdea.title: Inheritance rule
keyIdea.text: Use base classes to collect shared state and behavior; design bases with a focused contract to keep derived classes clean.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Inheritance
Definition

A derived class is built from a base class and automatically receives its properties and functions, forming an "is-a" relationship used to group related game objects.

Example
AEnemy defines Health and Attack(); AZombieEnemy inherits those members and adds zombie-specific effects.
Common misconception

Inheritance is not just for reuse. It models relationships and enables polymorphism. Avoid placing unrelated features in one base class.

Key Takeaway

Design narrow base classes that capture shared behavior and a clear contract for derived types.

Hierarchy example
UObject
Base engine object
AActor
World presence, lifecycle hooks
ACharacter
Movement and input for characters
Use this pattern in your code: place shared fields and helper methods in a focused base class, then override or extend behavior in derived classes where necessary.

screens.title: Polymorphism and dynamic dispatch
screens.subtitle: How Unreal uses virtual functions to pick implementations at runtime

narration.text: Polymorphism lets different concrete objects be treated through a common base interface, and dynamic dispatch selects the correct implementation at runtime. In Unreal C++ this is achieved with virtual functions. When a function in a base class is marked virtual, the compiler sets up the necessary support so that a call through a base-class pointer invokes the derived override appropriate to the actual object. For example, if you have a TArray of AEnemy pointers and that array contains AZombieEnemy and ASpiderEnemy instances, a loop that calls Attack() on each AEnemy pointer will execute the zombie attack for zombies and the spider attack for spiders without the loop needing any type checks. A common misconception is believing polymorphism comes from pointers themselves; pointers only reference objects — the runtime selection happens because of virtual functions. Another important point: always use pointers or references for polymorphic objects; passing by value causes object slicing and loses the derived portion of the object. This is why game code commonly stores actor pointers in arrays and properties. Practically, design base interfaces for behaviors you know will vary, and make those functions virtual so you can swap implementations without changing callers.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism rule
keyIdea.text: Mark base methods virtual when derived types need to provide their own implementation and call through base pointers or references.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Polymorphism
Concept

Treat different concrete types through a shared base type and rely on the runtime to dispatch the correct implementation when functions are virtual.

Concrete example
// Manager.cpp (excerpt)
TArray<AEnemy*> ActiveEnemies;
// populate array with AZombieEnemy and ASpiderEnemy instances
for (AEnemy* Enemy : ActiveEnemies)
{
  if (Enemy)
  {
    Enemy->Attack(); // Calls derived Attack() at runtime
  }
}
Note how the loop contains no type checks or switch statements. The decision about which Attack() to run happens at runtime because Attack() is virtual in the base class.
Tips & pitfalls
  • Always use pointers or references for polymorphic objects to avoid slicing.
  • If base functions are not virtual, derived overrides will not be called through base pointers.
  • Keep base interfaces focused to reduce accidental breaking changes.
Key Takeaway

Polymorphism reduces branching and centralizes the call site while delegating variant behavior to derived classes.

screens.title: Virtual functions in Unreal C++
screens.subtitle: Declare virtual functions in a base class and override them in derived classes

narration.text: Virtual functions are the mechanism C++ uses to support runtime dispatch. In Unreal we often pair UFUNCTION with virtual so that both engine-level reflection and C++ polymorphism can coexist. A base class AEnemy might declare virtual void Attack(); so derived classes can provide their own Attack implementation. When Attack is called through an AEnemy pointer, C++ uses the virtual table to select the correct overridden method. It is important to separate declaration from implementation: the base class provides the declaration and possibly a default implementation; derived classes override that implementation to vary behavior. A common pattern in Unreal is to declare UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) virtual void Foo(); so designers can also expose the function to Blueprints. Remember that virtual is a compile-time modifier that creates runtime behavior. A frequent misconception is that virtual adds extra work for every call; in practice the cost is small compared to the architectural benefits in gameplay code. When you write virtual methods, document expected behavior and contracts so derived implementers know how to extend them correctly. Finally, avoid changing function signatures in derived classes: that causes hiding instead of overriding and breaks polymorphism.

keyIdea.title: Virtual function pattern
keyIdea.text: Declare shared behaviors as virtual in the base, optionally provide a default, and override in derived classes to change behavior at runtime.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Virtual Functions
Base declaration
// Enemy.h (excerpt)
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AEnemy : public AActor
{
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Combat")
  virtual void Attack();
};
Derived override
// ZombieEnemy.h (excerpt)
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AZombieEnemy : public AEnemy
{
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Combat")
  virtual void Attack() override;
};
Using override communicates intent and lets the compiler catch mismatches between base and derived signatures, preventing silent hiding bugs.

screens.title: Pure virtual functions and abstract classes
screens.subtitle: Force derived classes to implement required behavior

narration.text: A pure virtual function is declared with an equals-zero syntax in C++ and signals that the base class defines an interface but no concrete implementation for that function. In the chapter we see virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) = 0; in AEnemy. Declaring a pure virtual function makes the class abstract: the compiler prevents creating instances of the base class. This is useful when you want to ensure every concrete type implements a behavior, for example ensuring all enemies implement TakeDamage. The advantage is a strong contract — derived classes must provide an implementation so callers can rely on that method existing. A common misunderstanding is that abstract classes can be used as utility containers; instead treat them as a formal interface plus shared helper code only if defaults make sense. If you want a default implementation but still allow overriding, provide a normal virtual function with a body. Use pure virtual when you need to force derived classes to implement behavior relevant to gameplay. In Unreal, this pattern helps enforce consistent gameplay semantics across many actor types and keeps manager code simple because it can call methods that every derived type implements.

keyIdea.title: Abstract class benefit
keyIdea.text: Use pure virtual functions to define mandatory behavior that every derived class must implement, producing reliable contracts for gameplay systems.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Pure Virtuals
Pure virtual example
// Enemy.h
virtual void TakeDamage(float DamageAmount) = 0; // pure virtual

This makes AEnemy abstract. No AEnemy instances can be created. Derived enemies must implement TakeDamage.

When to use
  • When a behavior is required of all derived types.
  • When you want to enforce a contract at compile-time.
  • When a default implementation would be misleading or impossible.
Analogy

Think of an abstract class as a blueprint that lists required rooms but does not furnish them — derived classes must add the furniture.

screens.title: Weapon example: base and derived classes
screens.subtitle: Create AWeapon, ARifle, and APistol to demonstrate polymorphism

narration.text: Let's step through the hands-on weapon example from the chapter so you can reproduce it in your project. First, create a base AWeapon class that declares a virtual Fire method. The base can provide a default message or an empty implementation. Next, create ARifle and APistol derived from AWeapon and override Fire() using the override keyword. In their implementations, call the engine's on-screen debug or logging functions so you can see distinct messages when Fire is called. Finally, create a manager actor with a TArray of AWeapon pointers, populate it with rifle and pistol instances placed in the level or spawned at BeginPlay, and loop through the array calling Fire() on each pointer. This demonstrates polymorphism: the manager calls one interface and the runtime runs the appropriate derived Fire implementation. When reproducing this example in your project, ensure that Fire is declared virtual in AWeapon and that you use pointers in the array. If you forget virtual or use value semantics, the manager will not invoke the derived behavior. This example is compact, repeatable, and maps directly to common gameplay systems like weapon loadouts and ability systems.

keyIdea.title: Practical pattern
keyIdea.text: Define a virtual method in a base actor, override it in derived actors, then call through base pointers to trigger derived behavior at runtime.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Weapon Example
AWeapon (header)
// Weapon.h (excerpt)
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AWeapon : public AActor
{
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Weapon")
  virtual void Fire();
};
ARifle override
// Rifle.h (excerpt)
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API ARifle : public AWeapon
{
  GENERATED_BODY()
public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Weapon")
  virtual void Fire() override;
};
WeaponManager iteration
// WeaponManager.cpp (excerpt)
for (AWeapon* Weapon : WeaponsInInventory)
{
  if (Weapon)
  {
    Weapon->Fire(); // Calls Rifle or Pistol Fire() at runtime
  }
}
Use this pattern to keep managers generic and make adding new weapon types require only a new derived class with Fire() implemented.

screens.title: override keyword vs no override
screens.subtitle: Why using override prevents subtle bugs

narration.text: The override keyword is a simple, compiler-checked promise: you intend this function to override a virtual function in a base class. If the base signature changes or you mistype the derived signature, the compiler will produce an error instead of silently creating a new unrelated function. For example, writing virtual void Attack() override; in a derived class tells the compiler to confirm a matching virtual function exists in the base. Without override, a misspelled parameter or name can lead to function hiding, where calling Attack through a base pointer invokes the base implementation instead of the derived one. That bug can be very hard to find at runtime. Another contrast is between overriding a virtual function and hiding a non-virtual function with the same name: only the virtual case supports runtime polymorphism. Use override consistently in Unreal C++ classes where you mean to replace behavior. It is acceptable to omit override for functions that are not intended to override, but consistent use reduces cognitive load and prevents breaking changes from creeping in. Make it a habit: the slightly more verbose code saves debugging time later.

keyIdea.title: Safety tip
keyIdea.text: Use override so the compiler verifies your intention to override a base virtual function and catches signature mismatches early.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › override Keyword
With override
Derived signature must match base virtual signature. Compiler error if it doesn't.
virtual void Attack() override;
Without override
A typo or signature change can produce a new unrelated function and break polymorphism silently.
virtual void Atack(); // typo — silently compile
Key Takeaway

Prefer override whenever you intend to replace a base virtual method; it makes your intent explicit and the compiler your ally.

screens.title: Common mistakes: forgetting virtual and function hiding
screens.subtitle: Why polymorphism fails when base functions are not virtual

narration.text: A frequent source of confusion is function hiding: if you expect derived behavior but the base class function is not marked virtual, calling the function through a base-class pointer will always select the base implementation. This happens because C++ resolves non-virtual calls statically. You might write a derived Attack with a matching name and signature, but without virtual on the base, the derived version won't be used via a base pointer. Another common mistake is attempting to instantiate an abstract class that contains a pure virtual method — the compiler will prevent this and report an error. Fixing it requires implementing the pure virtual methods in derived classes. Finally, object slicing occurs when you pass a derived object by value into a function expecting a base object; the derived-specific data is sliced off and polymorphism is lost. Game programmers often store and pass pointers to avoid slicing. To prevent these issues, mark intended base functions as virtual, use override in derived classes, and keep interactions in your systems using pointers or references. This combination ensures the runtime behaves as you expect and avoids subtle bugs that only appear during gameplay testing.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these traps
keyIdea.text: If polymorphism behaves incorrectly, check for missing virtual on the base, missing override, and inadvertent value semantics causing object slicing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Common Mistakes
Missing virtual

If base methods are not virtual, derived overrides won't be called through base pointers. This causes unexpected base behavior at runtime.

Function hiding

A signature mismatch in the derived class creates a new function rather than overriding. Use override to catch this at compile time.

Object slicing

Passing derived objects by value to functions expecting a base value slices off derived data. Use pointers or references for polymorphic types.

Instantiating abstract classes

Attempting to create an instance of a class with pure virtual methods produces a compiler error. Implement required methods in derived classes instead.

screens.title: Unreal lifecycle functions and virtual methods
screens.subtitle: Why BeginPlay, Tick, and similar hooks are virtual

narration.text: Unreal Engine declares many lifecycle hooks as virtual so game code can provide per-type behavior without the engine needing to know every concrete type. For example, BeginPlay and Tick are virtual in AActor and UActorComponent, which allows you to override them in your derived actors to perform initialization, per-frame updates, and cleanup. When the engine calls these hooks through base pointers, the virtual mechanism ensures your actor's override runs. This design keeps engine code generic while giving flexibility to game authors. It also explains why overriding those lifecycle methods is so common in gameplay code — you provide the concrete behavior for spawn-time setup, physics updates, or per-frame logic. A misconception is that lifecycle methods must always call Super::BeginPlay() or Super::Tick(); while not always required, calling the base implementation preserves base-class functionality and avoids breaking engine or component-level behavior. As an architecture guideline, override lifecycle functions when you need actor-specific behavior, and call the base implementation unless you intentionally replace that behavior. This approach keeps derived classes composable and predictable in the engine's update loop. Unreal lifecycle functions and virtual methods means lifecycle hooks are virtual so derived actors can participate in engine-managed events; call the base implementation unless you explicitly replace it.. In practical terms, why beginplay, tick, and similar hooks are virtual. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Engine contract
keyIdea.text: Lifecycle hooks are virtual so derived actors can participate in engine-managed events; call the base implementation unless you explicitly replace it.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Lifecycle Hooks
Why they're virtual

Engine-managed events like BeginPlay and Tick must allow game code to supply actor-specific behavior. Declaring them virtual in base classes gives that flexibility.

When overriding, call Super::BeginPlay() or Super::Tick() unless you have a reason to replace the base behavior. Neglecting to call Super can break component initialization or engine assumptions in complex hierarchies.
Example
ACharacter overrides BeginPlay to set up animations; the engine calls BeginPlay on AActor pointers and the overridden implementation runs.
Key Takeaway

Lifecycle hooks are the sanctioned extension points of the engine; use them to place type-specific initialization and per-frame logic.

screens.title: Design pattern: base interface → derived implementations → manager
screens.subtitle: A simple pattern to apply polymorphism in gameplay systems

narration.text: A reliable pattern in Unreal is to define a small base interface, implement concrete derived classes, and write a manager that calls the interface methods on base pointers. This minimizes coupling and makes systems extensible. The process has three steps. First, design the base class to declare the virtual functions for the behaviors you expect to vary. Keep the base focused and avoid bundling unrelated functionality. Second, implement derived classes that specialize behavior by overriding those virtual functions and using override to ensure signature matches. Third, create a manager or system that stores base-class pointers — for example a TArray of AWeapon pointers — and uses a simple loop to call the interface method, relying on runtime dispatch to call the concrete implementation. This pattern reduces the need for conditionals and switch statements, and adding a new type requires only a new derived class. A common misconception is that this pattern forbids per-type data; it doesn't. Derived classes can hold specialized state and still be used through the base interface. When designing your systems, sketch the interface first and ask what must be common and what will vary.

keyIdea.title: Pattern summary
keyIdea.text: Define the contract in a base, implement variants in derived types, and operate on base pointers in a manager to get polymorphic behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Design Pattern
Three-step process
1. Base interface
Declare virtual methods that describe behaviors you need to call generically.
2. Derived implementations
Override the virtual methods with type-specific logic and state.
3. Manager calls
Store base pointers and call the interface method, letting the runtime dispatch to the correct implementation.
Example: AWeapon base, ARifle and APistol derived, AWeaponManager with TArray<AWeapon*> that iterates and calls Fire(). Adding new weapons requires no manager changes.
Check your understanding

Name one behavior in your project that could be moved into a base class to simplify managers and reduce conditionals.

screens.title: Compile and test: steps for the weapon lab
screens.subtitle: A concise runbook to verify polymorphic behavior in your level

narration.text: Follow this checklist while implementing the weapon activity to ensure your polymorphism works on the first run. Step one: create AWeapon as an AActor subclass and declare virtual void Fire() with UFUNCTION if you want Blueprint exposure. Step two: create ARifle and APistol inheriting from AWeapon and implement Fire() with override, using GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage or UE_LOG to write distinct messages so you can see behavior in the output log. Step three: create an AWeaponManager actor with a TArray property of AWeapon pointers editable in Details. Spawn or place instances of ARifle and APistol in the level, and assign them to the manager's array. Step four: in BeginPlay of the manager, iterate over the array and call Fire() on each pointer. Step five: compile and run; if you see the correct messages — "Rifle Fired" and "Pistol Fired" — polymorphism is working. If you see only the base message, re-check that Fire is declared virtual in AWeapon and that you used override in derived classes. Also verify you are using pointers in the array and not value objects. This short runbook helps you isolate common causes of failure quickly.

keyIdea.title: Testing checklist
keyIdea.text: Declare virtual in base, override in derived, use pointers in the array, and inspect engine logs to confirm derived methods run at runtime.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Compile & Test
Runbook
  1. Create AWeapon and declare virtual Fire().
  2. Make ARifle and APistol and override Fire() using override.
  3. Create AWeaponManager with TArray<AWeapon*> and populate with instances.
  4. Call Fire() on each pointer in BeginPlay and check logs.
  5. If behavior is wrong, check for missing virtual, missing override, or value semantics.
Quick debug tips
  • Use distinct on-screen messages per derived Fire() to verify which implementation runs.
  • Ensure WeaponsInInventory stores pointers to actors, not class types unless you spawn them.
  • Use the compiler errors from override to find signature mismatches quickly.
Key Takeaway

A short checklist and clear debug messages will usually reveal the cause of polymorphism failures within minutes.

screens.title: Key Concepts — part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to retain. First, inheritance creates an "is-a" hierarchy that shares data and behavior across related types, which reduces duplication and clarifies design. Second, polymorphism allows you to write code against base-class interfaces and let the runtime invoke the appropriate derived implementation using virtual functions. Third, virtual versus pure virtual is an important distinction: virtual methods can have defaults in the base and be overridden; pure virtual methods make the base abstract and force derived classes to implement the contract. Keep these three ideas in your toolbox and look for opportunities to apply them in enemy types, weapons, and collectible systems. Use focused base classes to avoid monolithic designs, and prefer pointers or references for polymorphic objects. When you write your own systems, pick one area to refactor into a base and derived classes as practice.

keyIdea.title: Memory aid
keyIdea.text: Inheritance for structure, polymorphism for behavior, and virtual/pure virtual to control flexibility and contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts
Inheritance
Create a base that captures shared state and let derived classes specialize behavior.
Polymorphism
Call methods through base pointers and let the runtime choose the derived implementation via virtual dispatch.
Virtual vs Pure Virtual
Virtual allows defaults; pure virtual forces derived classes to implement the method and makes the base abstract.
Summary
Design narrow base classes, mark varying behavior virtual, use override, and operate on pointers to preserve polymorphism.

screens.title: Key Concepts — part 2
screens.subtitle: Three practical reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you implement, remember these practical reminders. First, always prefer pointers or references for polymorphic objects to avoid object slicing — value semantics remove derived-specific data. Second, use the override keyword in derived classes to let the compiler validate that you are correctly overriding a base virtual method. Third, test polymorphism with clear, distinct debug messages in derived implementations so you can easily see which implementation runs at runtime. These small habits reduce debugging time and make your codebase easier to extend. When you return to your project, pick one system to refactor into a base plus derived types and apply these reminders as you code and test — you'll get immediate benefits in clarity and extensibility. Key Concepts — part 2 means avoid slicing, use override, and check logs with distinct messages to verify polymorphism quickly.. In practical terms, three practical reminders before you code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical checklist
keyIdea.text: Avoid slicing, use override, and check logs with distinct messages to verify polymorphism quickly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts — Practical
Use pointers
Pointers preserve derived data and enable polymorphism; avoid passing polymorphic objects by value.
Use override
Make your intent explicit so the compiler can catch mismatches between base and derived signatures.
Verify with logs
Use distinct on-screen messages or log lines in derived methods to confirm polymorphic dispatch during testing.
Final thought
Small habits like override and pointer-based arrays yield large dividends in maintainability and correctness for gameplay systems.
